title: How do we find three products quickly?
description: Three products are found quickly by pairing numbers that make a hundred or a thousand, and by writing one hundred twenty five as a thousand divided by eight. Each answer is then checked by another route.
teaching_notes: One idea: look for numbers that pair up to a round number, and rewrite an awkward factor as a division of a round number. Ask the class which two numbers in the first product pair up before any work is shown. Watch for students who multiply left to right and never look for a pair.

video_script.why: The child has seen times five as times ten then half, and now looks for pairs that make round numbers and for a factor that is a round number divided by something.
video_script.substitution: Pair factors that make 100 or 1000, and write 125 as 1000 ÷ 8, then multiply and divide the round numbers.
video_script.anchor: Three products written in a column: 2 × 1768 × 50, then 72 × 125 with the hint 125 = 1000 ÷ 8, then 125 × 40 × 8 × 25.
video_script.payoff_line: Each product was found with a quick pair or a division

final_answer.spoken: one lakh seventy six thousand eight hundred, nine thousand and ten lakh

never_show: a final product before the answer beat
maths_rules: checks: 1768 < 2000 so the first is a little less than 2000 × 100; 125 × 70 + 125 × 2 = 8750 + 250 = 9000; 3 zeros + 3 zeros = 6 zeros, 10,00,000
video_script.design: One idea: pair factors to round numbers and rewrite 125 as 1000 divided by 8. The anchor stays all video; the working band builds in the idea part; no hard clear.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We must find quick ways to calculate three products.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The first is two times one thousand seven hundred sixty eight times fifty.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The second is seventy two times one hundred twenty five. The book hints that one hundred twenty five is one thousand divided by eight.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>The third is one hundred twenty five times forty times eight times twenty five.
<bookmark mark='m6'/>How can we calculate each one quickly?

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Some pairs of numbers multiply to give a round number such as one hundred or one thousand.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two times fifty makes one hundred, and eight times one hundred twenty five makes one thousand.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Forty times twenty five also makes one thousand, and multiplying by a round number only adds zeros.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>We work the same way as the shortcut examples in your book.

marks.m1: the given line is written in the working band

beats.on_screen: Step 1: 2 × 1768 × 50: pair 2 × 50 = 100; then 1768 × 100 = 1768 with two zeros after it

marks.m1: 2 and 50 are lit and joined by a pair mark
marks.m3: 1768 × 100 is written, and two zeros join the end of 1768

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, in the first product, pair two with fifty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two times fifty makes one hundred. What is left is one thousand seven hundred sixty eight times one hundred.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Two zeros join the end of the digits one seven six eight.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, in the second product, write one hundred twenty five as one thousand divided by eight.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Seventy two times one thousand is seventy two thousand.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Divide seventy two thousand by eight in two parts, sixty four thousand and eight thousand.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Sixty four thousand divided by eight is eight thousand, and eight thousand divided by eight is one thousand. We add the two parts.

marks.m1: 125 and 8 are joined by a pair mark
marks.m2: 40 and 25 are joined by a pair mark; both pairs show 1000

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, in the third product, pair one hundred twenty five with eight. That makes one thousand.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Pair forty with twenty five, and that also makes one thousand.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>What is left is one thousand times one thousand.

marks.m1: the word check is written above three check lines

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, check each answer by another route.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>For the first, two thousand times one hundred is a little more than our answer.
<bookmark mark='m2b'/>That is right, because one thousand seven hundred sixty eight is less than two thousand.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>For the second, add one hundred twenty five times seventy and one hundred twenty five times two.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>That is eight thousand seven hundred fifty plus two hundred fifty, which agrees. For the third, three zeros and three more zeros make six zeros in all.
